analysis.one_liner: Sets a $20 floor price on imported oil, with the surcharge funding oil reserves, efficiency programs, and low-income weatherization.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced beyond House subcommittees and died at the end of the 102nd Congress without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have put a $20 minimum price on imported oil. Whenever the average price of West Texas crude fell below $20 in a month, importers would pay a surcharge on every barrel and barrel-equivalent of imported oil brought in the following month. The money would flow into a new Energy Security Investment Fund to buy oil for the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (including home heating oil for storage in heating-oil-dependent regions), fund low-income home weatherization, and promote energy efficiency and domestic oil and gas recovery. The President could waive the surcharge for some Western Hemisphere oil producers, and would have to report to Congress on cooperating with those countries. The bill was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees, and never received any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic oil and gas producers gain the most: a $20 floor keeps prices from collapsing and protects them from cheap foreign crude, which the bill's own findings say was shrinking U.S. production. Low-income households gain through federally funded home weatherization, and regions dependent on home heating oil gain from a dedicated heating-oil reserve and efficiency programs paid for out of the fund.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Domestic oil producers and low-income households

how_it_helps.text: When the average West Texas crude price falls below $20 for a 30-day period, the bill requires the Secretary of Energy to calculate and certify a surcharge on imported crude (heading 2709.00) of the full shortfall and on imported petroleum products (heading 2710) of 110 percent of the shortfall, effective the following month.

All surcharge revenue is transferred quarterly into a dedicated Energy Security Investment Fund, which can be appropriated to buy crude and petroleum products — including home heating oil for storage in heating-oil-dependent regions — for the Strategic Petroleum Reserve.

The fund can also pay for low-income home weatherization and for Department of Energy programs promoting energy efficiency, commercializing efficient technologies, and improving domestic oil and gas recovery.

The President may waive the surcharge on crude from Western Hemisphere countries when doing so would enhance U.S. energy security and expand opportunities for U.S. oil and gas firms abroad, and must report to Congress on cooperation with Western Hemisphere producers.

analysis.who_pays: Users of gasoline, diesel, and fuel oil pay through higher prices whenever world oil falls below $20, since importers pass the surcharge on. The cost is effectively a variable tax on imported oil, borne by consumers at the pump and by households heating with oil, and by refiners and importers who rely on cheap foreign crude.

drawbacks.text: Whenever oil prices dip below $20, the surcharge raises the cost of gasoline, diesel, and heating oil for consumers — a cost that falls hardest on households that heat with oil, even as a share of the revenue goes back to low-income weatherization.

The floor price undermines the price signal that pushes consumers toward conservation and efficiency; the bill itself acknowledges that low prices were eroding annual energy-efficiency gains, yet its answer is to raise the price consumers pay rather than tax production broadly.

The Western Hemisphere waiver gives the President discretion to exempt favored producers from the surcharge and explicitly requires that waivers expand opportunities for U.S. oil and gas firms abroad, inviting pressure over which countries benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a genuinely mixed design. Its real consumer-facing benefits — a larger Strategic Petroleum Reserve with a heating-oil component, low-income weatherization, and efficiency programs — are paid for by a surcharge that raises fuel prices exactly when oil is cheap, which is when consumers most benefit from low prices. The largest beneficiary is the domestic oil industry, which gets a guaranteed price floor; the net effect on working households depends on how much weatherization and efficiency funding actually reaches them versus what they lose at the pump and on their heating bills.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees on trade and energy, and neither committee ever took it up, so it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Gephardt introduced the Energy Security and Price Stability Act of 1991 in the House on June 18, 1991, joined by five Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred jointly to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees on the day of introduction.
On June 24, 1991 it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Trade, and on August 13, 1991 to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Energy and Power.
No committee action, hearing, markup, or floor vote followed; the bill's last recorded action was the August 1991 subcommittee referral, and it expired when the 102nd Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers are arguably better off because the bill died: they avoided a surcharge that would have raised fuel prices whenever oil fell below $20. Domestic oil producers lost the chance at a price floor, and low-income weatherization and Strategic Petroleum Reserve funding were never created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fuel consumers; domestic oil producers lost out

for.name: Rep. Richard Gephardt
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 18, 1991, along with Reps. Fazio and Wise, proposing a $20 floor price on imported oil to fund the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, weatherization, and efficiency programs.

for.name: 5 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it its entire initial support within one party.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Energy and Power and never reported it out; no markup or hearing is recorded.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair Dan Rostenkowski (D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Trade and never acted on it; as the committee with jurisdiction over tariffs, its inaction alone was enough to stop the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote, so no measure of bipartisan or partisan support or opposition exists beyond that.

industries.note: A $20 floor on imported oil keeps domestic prices from falling below that level whenever world prices collapse, protecting domestic producers' revenue. That gain comes directly out of consumers' pockets at the pump and in home heating bills, though a share of the surcharge funds weatherization and efficiency for low-income households.

Importers and refiners of foreign crude and refined products would pay the surcharge directly on every barrel entered, raising their input costs. Their preference for cheap imports ran alongside consumers' interest in low fuel prices.

The bill creates a dedicated revenue stream for low-income home weatherization, efficiency commercialization, and related Department of Energy programs, expanding demand for these services. The funding depends entirely on surcharge collections when oil prices are low.

industries.industry: Domestic oil and gas service industries
industries.note: The Western Hemisphere waiver provisions require that waivers expand economic opportunities for U.S. oil and gas and related service firms abroad, and the fund supports enhanced domestic oil and gas recovery. These benefits are tied to a bill whose main revenue source is a consumer-borne import surcharge.
